issues.legal_issue: An undivided family is presumed joint unless the evidence establishes otherwise, and its head may represent it in a suit concerning family property.
material_facts: The claimants adduced evidence that the family remained undivided and that the first claimant was its head when the suit was instituted.
That evidence was unrebutted, and there was no evidence establishing that the family had divided.
issues.conclusion: The family was undivided, and the first claimant was its head when the suit was instituted.
issues.legal_principle: A Hindu family is presumed to be joint unless the contrary is established. The Court relied on that presumption and the unrebutted evidence; it cited no statutory provision or earlier case for this issue.

rule.if: family_property_recovery_suit and unrebutted_evidence_of_joint_family and no_evidence_of_division and evidence_of_claimant_as_family_head

predicates.family_property_recovery_suit: The proceeding seeks recovery of property claimed as belonging to a family.
predicates.unrebutted_evidence_of_joint_family: The claimant presented evidence that the family remained joint, and no opposing evidence rebutted it.
predicates.no_evidence_of_division: No evidence showed that the family had divided.
predicates.evidence_of_claimant_as_family_head: Evidence showed that the claimant was the family head when the suit was instituted.

issues.definition: When a family-property recovery suit is supported by unrebutted evidence that the family remained joint and that the claimant was its head, the claimant is authorized to represent the family.

issues.legal_issue: A person who advances money required to recover family property and takes possession through execution acquires a lien for the advance, while later transferees acquire no greater rights than that person held.
material_facts: A decree allowed recovery of the property upon payment of a sum to the prior possessor.
A relative paid that sum into court and took possession through execution, but received no sale deed or other transfer document.
The family members who obtained the decree were junior members and could not validly alienate the property.
Later purchasers acquired their claimed rights through the relative.
issues.conclusion: The person who advanced the money had only a lien over the property for the amount advanced, and later purchasers acquired no greater rights.
issues.legal_principle: The person who paid the amount required for recovery and took possession thereby had a lien securing reimbursement, not ownership. A transferee of that person's rights could acquire no greater right than the transferor held. The Court cited no statutory provision or earlier case for this issue.

rule.if: property_title_dispute and recovery_decree_required_payment and third_party_paid_recovery_amount and possession_taken_through_execution and no_transfer_document and transferors_lacked_authority_to_convey

predicates.property_title_dispute: The proceeding concerns competing claims to ownership or rights in property.
predicates.recovery_decree_required_payment: A decree made recovery of the property conditional on payment of an amount.
predicates.third_party_paid_recovery_amount: A person other than the decree-holders paid the amount required for recovery.
predicates.possession_taken_through_execution: The payer obtained possession through execution of the recovery decree.
predicates.no_transfer_document: No sale deed or other document transferring ownership to the payer was executed.
predicates.transferors_lacked_authority_to_convey: The persons who obtained the recovery decree lacked authority to convey ownership of the property.

issues.definition: Where a person pays the amount required by a recovery decree, takes possession through execution, and receives no transfer from persons able to convey ownership, that person and later successors have no greater property right than the payer's reimbursement lien.

issues.legal_issue: Permissive possession does not mature into adverse possession unless a hostile claim is asserted to the knowledge of the true owners for the requisite period.
material_facts: The property remained in the possession of the family's tenants.
The person who advanced the recovery amount and the later claimants could at most collect rent; their possession was, at most, symbolic and permissive because the initial possessor held a lien.
There was no evidence that any of those possessors asserted hostile title to the property to the knowledge of the true owners.
issues.conclusion: The possessors did not acquire title by adverse possession.
issues.legal_principle: Permissive possession cannot become adverse possession without proof that the possessor asserted a hostile title to the knowledge of the true owners for twelve years or more. The Court cited no statutory provision or earlier case for this issue.

rule.if: property_recovery_suit and permissive_possession and not hostile_claim_known_for_limitation_period

predicates.property_recovery_suit: The proceeding seeks recovery of property from persons claiming rights through possession.
predicates.permissive_possession: The possession began or continued with permission, including possession held only to secure reimbursement of an advance.
predicates.hostile_claim_known_for_limitation_perio: The possessor asserted a hostile title to the knowledge of the true owners for the requisite limitation period.

issues.definition: In a property-recovery suit, permissive possession without a hostile claim known to the true owners for the requisite period does not result in acquisition of title by adverse possession.
